Approach

How I work

  1. 01

    I design for constraints, not for portfolios.

    Legacy systems, regulatory requirements, engineering capacity, internal politics. Most of my work is deciding what not to build, and being able to explain why.

  2. 02

    I know this domain.

    Field service software fails in specific ways. Technicians work offline in basements and plant rooms. They wear gloves. They don't know what "Case" means in your ERP. If you've never watched someone try to close a job in the rain, you'll design the wrong thing.

  3. 03

    On AI.

    I use AI to compress execution: first-pass copy, code prototypes, synthesising research notes. I don't use it to decide what to build. The judgement is the job.

FSM Mobile UI Redesign

Empowering field service technicians with a more intuitive mobile experience.

Company
Next Technik
Role
UX/UI Designer, User Researcher
Team
1 PM, 4 Developers
Platform
Responsive hybrid app
Timeline
June 2021 – March 2023
Background

Learning an industry from zero

Field service technicians are the people who show up when your air conditioner breaks down in summer, when your office elevator stops working, or when a restaurant's refrigerator fails during dinner service.

When I joined Next Technik in 2021 as the company's first and sole UX/UI designer, I knew nothing about this industry. But looking back, that was actually helpful — I came with no assumptions about how things "should" work.

My first assignment was redesigning the mobile app these technicians relied on daily. I knew I couldn't design something useful without understanding their world first. So I started with the basics: learning from our internal team about the business model and our products, then talking directly to field technicians about their real-world challenges.

The product

NextService FSM

An application that integrates directly into NetSuite to extend its ERP capabilities for field service operations — one side for the office, one side for the field.

The Office

Scheduler

  • Assign tasks & set time
  • Dispatch data sync
The Field

Mobile app

  • Real-time status sync
  • Upload mobile data
The Challenge

A responsive hybrid app, stretched thin

The FSM mobile app runs across smartphones, tablets and laptops, with content customisable through NetSuite's Config. Field technicians use it daily to manage tasks, document job details, and fill out forms on-site — but the existing UI presented several critical usability issues that impacted their efficiency.

Research · Mobile User Interviews

Talking to the people on the tools

17
field technicians
12
companies
3
regions — US, AU, NZ

One-on-one interviews via Zoom, 45 minutes to 1.5 hours each, with a note-taker from the team and participants sharing their mobile screens live.

Key research findings

What technicians needed

Easier information finding & updating

Key information was difficult to locate and scan quickly. Technicians couldn't update incorrect addresses or contact details on site, and needed better search, sort and filter across upcoming and past jobs.

Reduced training requirements

Technicians struggled with NetSuite jargon like "Project, Case, Task, Job" and unclear statuses like "Pending Approval/Fulfillment." Sync status wasn't visible, and errors gave no way to recover.

Better documentation & preview

Complex dropdown forms made key fields like "Close Case" easy to miss. No copy & paste, no multi-photo upload, and input fields that weren't built for mobile.

Improved communication options

No way to message between technicians and dispatchers, limited customer communication, and no SMS templates or in-app notifications.

Research deliverable · Persona

Tom, 45

10+ years servicing HVAC systems

Lived in the same area almost his entire life. Standard hours 8am–4pm. Always wears glasses out in the field.

Pain points
  • Copies job details into email as a backup in case the app fails to save them
  • Refreshing his job list can take over 40 seconds — and he does it multiple times a day
  • Spends more time on the phone to the office than actually doing the job
Redesign

Iterative design, tested at every step

A structured five-phase approach, with internal and external testing built in along the way.

  1. 01

    Define Visual Direction

    Collaborated with the dev team to build a UI mood board and collect design references establishing the visual direction.

  2. 02

    Create UI Designs

    Translated research insights into design strategies across every core screen.

  3. 03

    Internal Testing

    Gathered feedback from 18 internal team members to catch usability issues early.

  4. 04

    User Validation

    Moderated usability testing with real field technicians across four countries.

  5. 05

    Design System

    Shipped a WCAG AA compliant design system to scale the new UI safely.

02 · New UI Designs

Translating research into design strategies

Problem

Information at your fingertips

Critical information was hard to find quickly while standing at a job site.

Approach
  • Date selector for quick day navigation
  • Redesigned task cards with clear hierarchy — priority, deadline, location
  • Added search, sort and filter
Screens: Task list, Map view, Job details
Problem

Make the invisible visible

Hidden sync status and unclear system states caused data-loss anxiety and confusion.

Approach
  • Persistent offline-mode indicator
  • Real-time sync status with badge counters
  • Clear error messages with recovery guidance and modal warnings
Screens: Task list, Job details, all forms
Problem

Forms that work on mobile

Complex forms led to errors and frustration, especially with gloves on.

Approach
  • Split required vs. optional fields into tabs
  • 44×44px minimum touch targets
  • Inline validation, prominent save/cancel
Screens: all forms
Problem

Reduce communication friction

Phone calls interrupted workflow; customer communication was limited.

Approach
  • Messaging between technicians and dispatchers
  • SMS templates for common scenarios
  • In-app notification system
Screens: Task list, new notification screen
Flow & scope

I mapped the current UI flow, pages and components against the existing design files to see what needed reskinning — login, job list, job details, map, and all form components — then redesigned with mobile-first principles and documented form guidelines for Customer Service consultants.

03 · Internal testing

18 internal team members reviewed the proposed designs, surfacing usability issues and validating decisions before testing with real users.

04 · User validation

Testing with real technicians

Remote, moderated usability tests with 9 real users across 4 countries — 60–75 minute sessions across two high-fidelity prototypes: an interactive dark theme, and a light theme showing the happy path.

Global navigation

A new date selector for task scheduling and visual task counters created a more intuitive navigation experience.

Task summary card

Checked the client's existing config and updated the task summary card to test additional UI that could be added in future.

Form experience

Segmented controls replaced dropdowns; new form elements added for name, explanation text, notifications and tooltips, with CTA buttons anchored at the end.

4.5:1 minimum text contrast 3:1 minimum UI component contrast 44×44px touch targets for gloved hands
User testing results

9 field technicians · 4 countries · Jun–Jul 2022

8/9
overall satisfaction — "highly positive"

"It's giving us more of the functionality that we've been asking for a while. More user friendly... it's really good."

Field technician, usability test

"Checklist is much improved. The submit button at the bottom makes much more sense. Like the error message."

Field technician, usability test

Areas for improvement

  • Refresh button position — users accidentally pressed it while scrolling; moved to a fixed top-right position.
  • Date selector visibility — some users didn't notice it; increased its visual prominence.
  • Map loading feedback — added a loading indicator to confirm the app was responding on slow connections.
05 · Final design & design system

A visual refresh, built to scale

The Product Manager wanted a gradual rollout, so Phase 1 was a visual refresh only — no new components, just updating the look and feel to reduce risk.

Colour system Typography Components Icons Spacing Documentation
Impact & Outcomes

Quantitative results

  • 30+ user interviews across 2 research phases (2021–2022)
  • Tested with 27 participants — 18 internal + 9 external users
  • Overall satisfaction rating: 8/9

Qualitative impact

  • "It's giving us more of the functionality that we've been asking for a while. More user friendly." — real user feedback
  • Reduced UI-related support inquiries

Business value

  • Improved field technician productivity
  • Enhanced user satisfaction across diverse industries
  • Established a scalable design foundation for future features

tramTRACKER Redesign

Reimagining Melbourne's most popular tram tracking app.

Type
Personal Project / UX Exercise
Role
UX/UI Designer, User Researcher
Platform
Android
Timeline
Nov 2016 – Jan 2017
Background

Redesigning something people already loved

tramTRACKER was one of Melbourne's most popular public transport apps, serving thousands of daily commuters who rely on it to catch trams across the city. As a frequent user myself, I encountered several usability issues that frustrated my daily commute. But redesigning such a widely-used app presented a unique challenge: any changes needed to preserve the features users already loved while addressing the pain points.

The app had a loyal user base who knew exactly where everything was. My challenge was to improve the experience without disrupting their established mental models and daily habits.

Research

Store reviews & street interviews

I collected reviews from Google Play and the App Store, then interviewed 6 people on the street — 5 waiting for trams, 1 riding one — to learn daily usage patterns and what information people valued most. Three distinct user types emerged, each with different needs.

"A list of stop names is stupid. I don't know the tram network, I don't know which suburb is after which."

App store review

"What we need is a map. You tap on the map where you want to go and it suggests a route and when you need to leave."

App store review

"Especially like the notification feature."

App store review

"[The tram alarm is] extremely unreliable and hardly ever accurate," and every upgrade reset user settings.

App store review
Defining the problems

Nearby & Favourites

A long list of stop names didn't help users find their tram — most switched to map mode instead. "Add to favourite" was hidden in a menu, and managing favourite groups wasn't easy to understand.

Routes & myTram

Choosing a tram line showed only a stop list, not real-time info. myTram asked users to enter a vehicle number to check arrival time — a strange, unintuitive ask.

More, and miscellaneous friction

Functions were scattered with no clear organisation. The mandatory tutorial annoyed users, the main menu sat too close to the ad banner (leading to accidental taps), and the app surfaced information — like tram vehicle style and A/C — that users didn't actually need.

Research deliverable · Personas

Frank

Age 34
Software salesperson

Drives his daughter to school, then visits clients across the CBD by tram to avoid parking. Familiar with the tram network.

Needs
  • Accurate, reliable wait times — his professional image depends on being on time

Joseph

Age 23
Waiter

Works rotating shifts at a café; his apartment is close to a tram stop, so he takes trams everywhere on his days off.

Needs
  • A simple way to find the route from home to wherever he's headed

Mei

Age 28
Boutique assistant, visiting from China

Uses Google Maps to get around when travelling overseas; comfortable with the main points of a conversation in English.

Needs
  • Easy, immediate access to Melbourne's sights within limited time and budget
Competitive analysis

I analysed PTV, Transit and Commutr against tramTRACKER. Transit had the highest rating (4.2, 32,897 ratings) with comprehensive search; PTV offered trip planning that tramTRACKER lacked. But tramTRACKER was the only app with both list and map favourites, and the most detailed stop information. The analysis pointed to one conclusion: strong information depth, but weak navigation structure and no trip planning.

The redesign

Four main features

Based on store reviews, user stories and the competitive analysis, I redesigned the flow around four features.

Nearby

Shows nearby routes to help users find the tram line, closest stop and — most importantly — the waiting time. Addresses commuters like Frank who need quick, accurate information.

Favourites

Keeps the existing data structure but reworks the interface to make managing personal content easier — preserving what existing users love while improving usability.

A to B

Directions for transit or walking, searchable by place, address or map point, with saved home and work locations — directly addressing Joseph's need for route planning.

Discover

Nearby sightseeing in map and list views, searchable by keyword with one-click transit directions — built for users like Mei who don't know Melbourne yet.

Information architecture

The launch page gives immediate access to all four features, balancing regular commuters who want familiar stops fast, occasional users planning routes, and tourists who need discovery.

Lo-fi prototyping

Main pages were sketched on paper and tested to check whether the new flow made sense. 4 out of 4 users found the functions easy to understand and the information clear.

Wireframes

Mid-fidelity wireframes built in Axure RP to work through interaction details ahead of stakeholder feedback.

Usability testing

An interactive InVision prototype was tested with 4 people to validate the design decisions. The familiar patterns borrowed from Google Maps reduced the learning curve while keeping tramTRACKER-specific features front and centre.

"The 'A to B' is easy because it looks like Google Maps."

Usability test participant

"I love the map which shows nearby attractions."

Usability test participant
High-fidelity visual design

Final mockups built in Sketch, applying a clean, modern visual language while keeping recognisable elements from the original app.

Reflection & key learnings

Designing for existing users is different

Redesigning a popular app meant constantly balancing improvement with familiarity. Users had established habits that couldn't be completely disrupted — I learned to tell which elements were truly problematic versus just different from my personal preferences.

The power of mapping user journeys

Building personas for Frank, Joseph and Mei showed me that one interface needed to serve multiple use cases. The four-feature structure came from recognising those different needs, rather than forcing everyone into a single workflow.

NaviKing 3D

Designing Taiwan's next-generation car navigation app with 3D maps technology.

Company
Kingwaytek
Role
Senior UX Designer / Design Team Lead
Team
PM, R&D, QA, Korean maps engine supplier
Platform
Android & iOS
Timeline
Oct 2012 – Jul 2014 (19 months)
Background & Challenge

A deadline-driven leap to 3D

My previous company, Kingwaytek, owned NaviKing — a very popular car navigation app in Taiwan. With revenue declining from 2011, our vice president demanded a next-generation product built on brand-new 3D maps technology from a Korean supplier.

To differentiate the new app, our team needed to address existing shortcomings, define a desirable role for the product, and make sure it met drivers' actual needs — while collaborating with a Korean 3D maps engine supplier to build entirely new search and map experiences from scratch.

The pressure was intense. Our VP set an aggressive deadline: launch in July 2013. In reality, the project took 19 months, shipping in July 2014, as we worked through building a completely new navigation experience on untested 3D mapping technology.

My role & responsibilities

As senior designer and design team lead, I led the UX work, producing all major deliverables and presenting them to the Product Owner. Working closely with our R&D lead and Project Manager, I translated user needs into detailed system requirements for map interaction, search and voice recognition — specifications our Korean technology supplier could build against within their 3D engine's constraints.

I collaborated with R&D to define system specs, helped QA test beta versions, and trained junior UX designers on research, user flows and prototyping. I also set up Google Analytics tracking to measure user behaviour after launch.

Research & Discovery

Balancing competing priorities

Interviews with our VP, plus Sales, Marketing, R&D and QA, revealed expectations that didn't always agree.

"Need to be done ASAP. Launch in July 2013."

Vice President

"It's not easy to find the Navigation simulation button when I want to showcase our app."

Sales team

Marketing wanted a larger speed-limit alert; R&D pitched a HUD (heads-up display), an improved map-browsing and 2D navigation UI, QR-code destination setup, and Android 4.0 native sharing — keen to use the new 3D tech while fixing known 2D issues.

User feedback analysis

Store reviews, complaint emails and call records surfaced what users actually wanted.

"Hope My Favourite of NaviKing can be synced with My Places of Google Maps... Even if I use an iPhone later, I don't need to reset those places again."

User feedback

"Voice control is waiting for too many seconds to start recognizing what I said! It easily puts some noise in and greatly reduces the accuracy rate."

User feedback

Other themes: wanting map data stored on an external SD card, more control over interface colours, and frustration that the page always scrolled back to the top after returning from a previous screen.

User research

Alongside two teammates, I interviewed 7 users with varying navigation-app experience and driving habits, documenting their profiles, behaviours, hardware usage and pain points.

User requirement analysis

I mapped users' goals against their reasons, behaviours and feelings to conclude what benefits they valued and what functions they needed. For "set a destination efficiently," for example, users valued multiple input methods because typing addresses was slow and error-prone — leading to requirements for voice control, favourite locations, recent destinations, and QR-code scanning.

Information architecture

Given the app's complexity, I documented the IA in Excel — categories, main pages, definitions, required APIs and implementation notes — detail that was essential for coordinating with our Korean maps supplier and internal R&D team.

Design Process

Prototyping under shifting constraints

Built in Axure RP, the prototype was our final deliverable to R&D and was revised repeatedly as we discovered technical limits in the 3D engine. It had to demonstrate more than static screens — how the map transitioned between 2D and 3D, how voice commands would interrupt navigation, how route alternatives appeared, and how drivers would interact with it while moving.

Google Analytics implementation

I set up page names and event tracking so we could see which features were actually used, where users got stuck, and what to prioritise post-launch.

Key design features

Smart search with a customised keyboard

A customised keyboard suggested places and addresses while typing, supporting both Zhuyin and English input and switching seamlessly. Typing "COST" immediately surfaced Costco locations across Taiwan.

Multiple route suggestions

Each suggested route showed distance, time and cost, with current speed colour-coded and road works or traffic jams marked along the way.

3D navigation view

The 3D engine rendered objects matching what drivers saw in the real world, making guidance easier to follow. A side panel showed upcoming road names and current speed — green for good, yellow for moderate, red for slow.

Project outcome

Launching imperfect, iterating to excellence

After 19 months of development, NaviKing 3D released on July 27, 2014 — even though our team didn't feel the product was mature enough to launch. VP-driven deadline pressure forced us to ship with known issues in the 3D rendering.

Initial reviews reflected that: 3D rendering was slow on older devices, buildings looked distorted at certain angles, and battery consumption was significantly higher than our previous 2D product.

Rather than defend our decisions, we listened. User reviews became our product roadmap — we prioritised the most-mentioned pain points, worked with our Korean supplier to optimise 3D rendering performance, added an easy 2D/3D toggle, and cut battery consumption. Six months of focused iteration paid off: users who'd complained about performance began praising how 3D landmarks helped them navigate complex highway interchanges — exactly the feature we'd envisioned from the start.

3.2★ → 4.1★

App store rating, launch to six months post-launch iteration.
